json.markdown:
# **Qwen3.8 27B Runs 2× Faster With MTP - But the Wrong Setting Makes It 5× Slower**

## **I benchmarked every MTP draft depth on an 24 GB GPU across Q4\_K\_M and Q4\_K\_XL. The sweet spot is 5.**

Alexander Salazar

[Alexander Salazar](https://medium.com/@malexandersalazar) Follow

## TL;DR

MTP on Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4 gives a genuine ~2× on a 4090: 48.5 → 96.2 t/s on K\_M, 46.3 → 84.2 t/s on K\_XL. The useful band for `draft_num_predict` is 2 to 5, and 5 is the pick: best on K\_M, best on K\_XL, best average, best worst case.

Above 5 both builds lose ground. Drafting more tokens does not raise how many get accepted per verification pass, so the extra drafts are pure cost.

Above 8 on K\_XL, or 11 on K\_M, you are actively destroying performance (up to 5.3× slower than not using MTP at all). Those two numbers are three apart, on the same model and the same card, and that is the whole reason **"use a low value" was never a sufficient answer** . The heavier quant breaks earlier. Your card will break somewhere else.

Seventeen Gigabytes of Weights Moved to Produce a Single Token (By Author, Powered by Gemini)

At 27B parameters and 4-bit weights on my RTX 4090, one decode step costs roughly **20.6 ms** and produces exactly one token. That is where my ~48 tokens/s comes from, and no amount of clever prompting changes it.

The trick behind speculative decoding is that the forward pass is bound by memory bandwidth, not by compute. You are dragging seventeen gigabytes of weights across the memory bus to produce a single token. If you happened to have several *candidate* tokens sitting there, you could verify all of them in that same pass for nearly no extra cost, because the weights are already in flight.

Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is where those candidates come from. [unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF) ships with a small head trained to guess the next few tokens. The head drafts, the full model verifies. Every draft that matches what the model would have produced anyway is a free token. Every draft that doesn't is thrown away, and you fall back to the one token you were going to get regardless.

Two things follow, and both matter for the rest of this article.

**First, MTP is not a quality tradeoff.** The verification step is what makes it safe: a drafted token only survives if the main model agrees with it. NVIDIA's primer on the technique puts it plainly: when the draft is wrong, the target model just decodes normally, so [the output is not degraded](https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/large-language-models/latest/advanced-use-cases/speculative-decoding.html) . This is not quantization. You are not trading precision for speed. You are trading VRAM for speed.

**Second, it is not free.** The draft head has to live in memory, the drafted tokens have to be generated, and the verification pass has to chew through all of them whether they are accepted or not. On the Unsloth model card, the MTP module for Qwen3.8-27B ships as a single Q4\_0 file of about **1.37 GB** (no separate MTP build per quantization). You download the same module whether you run UD-Q4\_K\_M, UD-Q4\_K\_XL or anything else, and it costs the same gigabyte and change either way.

On a 24 GB card, 1.37 GB is not pocket money. That is the whole tension.

## 1. The problem: everybody says "low," nobody says how low

`draft_num_predict N` is the knob. It tells the runtime how many tokens to draft per verification pass. `N=0` turns MTP off.

When I went looking for a starting value, every source agreed on the shape of the advice (keep it small, more is not better) and disagreed on the number.

Recommended Draft Depth by Source, and the Range They Span (By Author)

One, two, three, five, six. All of them are "low." All of them come from people who know exactly what they are doing. The spread between smallest and largest is a factor of six, and every one of those pages tells you, correctly, that the right answer depends on your hardware.

Unsloth is the most explicit: try 1 through 6, keep whichever is fastest, and do not assume their starting number is optimal because [performance is hardware-dependent](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/mtp) .

Honest advice, and completely unsatisfying, because it hands the problem straight back to you. And there was a second axis nobody was testing: **does the answer change between quantizations of the same model?** K\_M and K\_XL are the same weights with different bit allocations, about a gigabyte apart on disk. On a card where a gigabyte is 4% of the total budget, that is not obviously a rounding error.

So: two open questions, no answers, and a 4090 doing nothing at night.

## 2. How many values? Yes

I could not sleep with this open. If I could not sleep, my computer wasn't going to either.

I built both quants at the same context size, wrote a harness that walks `draft_num_predict` from 0 to 15, three runs at each value, same prompt set every time, and left it running. Sixteen depths × two quants × three runs = 96 runs.

Sixteen is more than anybody recommends testing. That is the point. Every guide says sweep 1 through 6; but if the useful range really ends around 6, I wanted to see *what the other side of the wall looks like* , because "don't go past 6" and "past 6 your machine turns into a potato" are very different warnings, and only one of them makes you double-check your Modelfile before you walk away for the night.

## 3. The setup

## 3.1. The machine

Intel Core i7-14700KF with 128 GB RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM) running on Ubuntu 24.04 with Ollama. Flash attention on, `q8_0` KV cache, `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1` . That is the whole daemon-level story. Everything else that could move a number lives in the Modelfile below.

## 3.2. The sixteen builds

In Ollama the MTP head is a DRAFT instruction in the Modelfile, not a second FROM. One line, pointing at the [Q4\_0](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF?show_file_info=MTP%2Fmtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_0.gguf) module you downloaded alongside the weights:

```
FROM ./Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf
DRAFT ./mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_0.gguf
PARAMETER num_ctx 98304
PARAMETER num_batch 512
PARAMETER temperature 1.0
PARAMETER top_p 0.95
PARAMETER top_k 20
PARAMETER min_p 0.0
PARAMETER presence_penalty 0.0
PARAMETER repeat_penalty 1.0
PARAMETER draft_num_predict 5
```

Sixteen depths meant sixteen builds: same two .gguf files, one `PARAMETER draft_num_predict` apart, each tagged with its own depth so the harness could walk them by name.

Thirty-two builds for the MTP benchmark (By Author)

Thirty-two builds, actually (sixteen depths per quant). And there is the gigabyte the rest of this article turns on, sitting in the SIZE column: 17 GB against 18 GB.

## 3.3. What I held constant

**Sampling.** Exactly as Qwen recommends for this family: the values in the Modelfile above, identical across all sixteen builds.

**96K of context.** Just because I can load *either* quant, with the MTP module resident, and stay fully on the GPU. MTP eats VRAM like everything else. In my experience, the moment any part of this model spills to CPU the measurement stops being about MTP and starts being about round-trip latency, and a benchmark that silently changes what it is measuring halfway through a sweep is worse than no benchmark.

**No vision projector.** I left the mmproj out to keep this to one variable.

## 3.4. The benchmark

All sixteen model configurations received the same instruction:

```
You are a technical writing benchmark generator. Write a long, continuous,
detailed explanation of how transformer-based LLMs decode text, including
attention, KV cache, sampling, batching, and token prediction. Do not use
markdown. Do not stop early. Continue with as much concrete detail as possible.
```

Prose, not code, and markdown explicitly disabled (one text distribution across the whole sweep), so nothing downstream is a formatting artifact.

**The measurement.** Completion tokens divided by the streaming window, where the window starts at the **first token** , not at the request. Prefill and model load are excluded by construction, so what you are looking at is decode throughput and nothing else. Time to first token is recorded separately, from request start to first streamed character.

Four details that make the numbers worth arguing about:

- **A 16-token warmup runs before every measured call and is thrown away.** No cold-load contamination anywhere in the sweep.
- **Model order is shuffled every epoch.** If the room warms up, or the card throttles, or something drifts over eight hours of running, it does not land systematically on whichever model happened to be last in the list.
- **Stopping is adaptive, not fixed.** The harness keeps running epochs until every model has the same number of successful runs, there are no errors, and the cumulative generated volume across models agrees within 5% of the median (tolerating at most one outlier beyond 2σ). Minimum three epochs, maximum ten. It converged at three, which is why every point here is n=3.
- **Failures abort, they do not get papered over.** Two retries per call; if a model still fails, the run stops rather than write a partial epoch and quietly break the equal-run-count invariant. Every configuration in this article has three successes and zero errors.

## 3.5. What the numbers are not

Three limits worth stating up front:

- **Not long-context measurements.** Time to first token sits around 316 ms across the sweep, which tells you the prompt is short relative to the window. The models are *configured* for 96K; the prompt did not fill it. Everything here is decode-bound behavior.
- **Not your numbers.** Absolute throughput on your machine will differ with card, driver, thermals and whatever else you have open. The community sweep linked above says it better than I can: the deltas are the durable part, not the absolutes.
- **Not instrumented for VRAM.** I confirmed the GPU/CPU split was 100% GPU for every configuration before each run, but I did not record it per configuration alongside the throughput numbers. Nothing here spilled to CPU; I just can't hand you the table.

The harness is standard library only (no dependencies, no framework), one file. If you want to reproduce this on your own card, [**here you are**](https://gist.github.com/malexandersalazar/389fbd961508c448888ce06c7b8b5b79) .

## 4. The whole curve

Decode Throughput as a Function of Speculative Draft Depth for Two 4-Bit Quantizations (By Author)

Both quants climb hard, peak around N=5, and then fall off a cliff into a region where **enabling MTP is worse than never having touched it.** Not slightly worse. At N=15 the K\_XL build runs at 8.7 t/s against a 46.3 t/s baseline (a **5.3× slowdown** ), with the model 100% resident on the GPU throughout (verified, not assumed). This is not spilling. It is the drafting itself.

The good half first:

Peak Throughput and Speedup at N=5, Both Quants (By Author)

Roughly double, on both quants. That sits squarely inside the range Unsloth publishes for MTP on this family, so no surprise there. The surprise is everything to the right of the peak.

## 5. Where MTP stops paying

Speedup Relative to Disabled Speculation Across Draft Depths (By Author)

Here is the answer to the question I actually started with, and it is not a single number.

**K\_XL goes underwater at N=8. K\_M holds out until N=11.**

Same model. Same machine. Same prompt. Same night. The only difference is about a gigabyte of weights, and it is worth **three steps of** **`draft_num_predict`** .

That is the part I had not seen written down anywhere, and it changes how you should read every recommendation in that table. "Use a low value" is not a property of the model. It is a property of the model *and the quantization and the card and how much room is left after your context.* A depth that is comfortable on K\_M can already be past break-even on K\_XL, on the identical machine, on the same afternoon.

If you take one thing from this article: **the safe depth is not a constant you can copy from a docs page. It moves with your build.**

## 6. What the measurements actually say

Forget the fit for a moment. Here is every candidate depth, as speedup over MTP off, on both builds (plus the average of the two) and, more usefully, the *worse* of the two, because on an unknown machine the floor matters more than the ceiling.

Speedup at Every Candidate Depth, With Mean and Worst Case Across Builds (By Author)

**N=5 wins outright, four times over.** Best on K\_M. Best on K\_XL. Best average. Best worst case. There is no criterion in this dataset under which something else is preferable.

The two curves do not agree equally well, and that is worth being precise about. K\_XL rises monotonically (1.43, 1.59, 1.65, 1.74, 1.82) and tops out cleanly at 5. K\_M is jagged: it swings 0.3× or more between adjacent depths across the whole healthy band, which is more movement than the 5% separating its own peak from N=2. So the clean read on N=5 comes from K\_XL, and K\_M agrees with it without being able to resolve it on its own. Two builds landing in the same place is worth something. It is not two independent measurements.

One caveat on reading the ordering too closely: K\_M dips to 1.50× at N=4, but K\_XL's N=4 is 1.74×, its second-best value in the sweep. The builds disagree there, which is the signature of run-to-run noise rather than a property of the depth. Anywhere from 2 to 5 is a defensible setting. Below 2 you are leaving speed on the table; above 5 you are paying for drafts nobody accepts.

So: **the useful band is 2 to 5, the pick is 5.**

## 7. The bill you pay on first-token latency

Time to First Token as a Function of Speculative Draft Depth (By Author)

Time to first token is **flat at around 316 ms from N=0 through N=7** on both builds. In the healthy region, drafting costs you nothing on latency. You get the throughput and pay no entry fee.

Then it climbs: 526 ms on K\_M at N=15 (+66%), 624 ms on K\_XL (+97%). And look at *where* it starts climbing: K\_XL departs at N=8, K\_M at N=11. The same two numbers as the throughput cliff. Two independent metrics pointing at the same boundary is the closest thing to corroboration this dataset has.

The practical use: **first-token latency is a free early-warning signal.** If it starts rising as you raise N, you have already gone too far. You do not need to wait for a throughput measurement to tell you.

## 8. When to use MTP at all

This is the part the throughput numbers cannot answer, because on a 24 GB card MTP and context length draw from the same account. The draft module and its buffers are gigabytes you are not spending on KV cache. So "should I enable MTP" is really "what am I selling to pay for it," and the answer depends on how you work.

I split my own AI-assisted development into two modes, and they want opposite things.

## 8.1. Unattended: the agent is working, I am not

Unattended: the agent is working, I am not (By Author, Powered by Gemini)

I hand over a plan, a checklist, a set of specs, and I go do something else. The agent decomposes the work, spawns subagents, moves through tasks, updates state, and I read the result later.

Here the scarce resource is **context, not speed.** The agent needs room for the plan, the checklist, its own reasoning, the files it is touching, and the output it is about to write on top of all that. When it runs out it compacts, and if the window is too small it compacts so often that it never gets a clear run at the actual feature: **you end up in a loop where nothing finishes** . Meanwhile nobody is watching the tokens stream. The difference between 48 t/s and 96 t/s costs me nothing, because I am not in the room. Trading a gigabyte and a half of context for speed I will never observe is a bad deal.

**Unattended work: keep the context. Skip MTP.**

## 8.2. Attended: I am in the loop, and I am the one waiting

Attended: I am in the loop, and I am the one waiting (By Author, Powered by ChatGPT)

This is babysitting mode. I am prompting in Claude Code or OpenCode, referencing the specific files that matter, defining the boundaries of the task myself: clearly and comprehensively, because in this mode that is my job.

Here the context requirement is genuinely smaller, and not as a compromise. When I review code I would rather read ten to twenty files properly than have something skim two hundred and hand me a summary. Or worse: watch a test suite I did not write go green over coverage I never checked, and push to main with a sense of safety I have not earned. Ten files I actually understand beats two hundred I have merely been *near* .

So the window is small on purpose, and the bottleneck moves somewhere completely different: **to me, watching tokens appear.** Every second of decode is a second of my attention burning. Doubling throughput here does not save the machine any work, it saves *mine* , and it is the difference between a tight iteration loop and one where I alt-tab away and lose the thread entirely.

**Attended work: take the speed. Enable MTP.**

The general principle, if you want one: **MTP converts VRAM into decode speed. That is a good trade exactly when a human is waiting on the tokens, and a bad one when a machine is.**

# Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 40 tokens/second on an M4 Max MacBook, 4.27 bpw quant, 244k context

Andrew Zhu

Andrew Zhu Follow

I have been running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on my Linux box for weeks now. It is a startlingly good model - in day-to-day use it feels more thoughtful than Qwen3.8-27B, and the 27B was already good enough that I had stopped looking for alternatives. Flash-Next is better in almost every way. The one thing it takes back with the other hand is size, and the decode speed that size costs you.

So here is the verdict up front, before you decide whether to keep reading. On a 64 GB M4 Max MacBook Pro, with a 4.27 bpw quant, a separate multi-token-prediction head, and 168,000 tokens of context, I am getting **30-40 tokens/second decode** . Not "demo-able." Not "good enough for a paragraph." Actual coding-agent, long-document, all-day driver speed. It cost me a night of dead ends and about a dozen failed launches to get there.

It is not free. The laptop loses to my RTX cards on prefill, and the setup is fussy in three specific places that nobody warns you about. Those three places are the whole article.

## Why bother when I already have GPUs

On my Linux machine, with 3 RTX 3090 + one RTX 3070 Ti Ampere cards, Flash-Next with MTP peaks around 65 tokens/second, and settles into 35-40 tokens/second once the context grows past 50k. That is a good number.

It is also a space heater. The published board power of those cards is around 300w, which is north of a kilowatt under load. The model is running most of the day. The bill notices.

I wanted the same brain in a machine that idles at single-digit watts and doesn't need its own circuit. Say, a 64 GB M4 Max.

At a glance the idea is absurd: the weights I run on the Linux box are bigger than the laptop's entire memory. But after more errors than I care to admit, I got it running with 168k context, holding 30-40 tokens/second. Here is how.

## Step 0: raise the ceiling on how much RAM the GPU is allowed to touch

By default, Apple caps how much memory the GPU may wire. On a 64 GB machine llama.cpp will look at your 64 GB and politely use about 56 GB of it, because Metal reports a `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` derived from a kernel reserve. For machines above 32 GB, Apple reserves 25% of installed RAM; the source is `AGXAccelerator::calcMaxGPUPhysicalMemoryBytes` , and the value is what llama.cpp compares against before it hands you an out-of-memory.

Raise it:

```
sudo sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb=61440    # 60 GiB, and it resets on reboot
```

Do this before you launch anything. Processes read `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` once at startup and cache it, so a limit raised after launch does nothing for the running server.

**Can you go higher? No.** I want to be blunt here, because the failure mode at this specific limit is not an error message. Wired pages are the one class of memory the kernel cannot compress, page out, or reclaim. Apple's own reserve rule and the community guidance point the same direction: leave at least 4 GB for the operating system and WindowServer.

Push past it and you don't get a crash you can catch. You get a kernel-level fault: the cursor stops, fans spin up, and unsaved work goes with it. People run 120 GB caps on 128 GB machines because those machines have 8 GB to spare. You do not.

The other reason is that a bigger number doesn't buy you model weights, it buys you *permission to thrash* . The moment your GPU-wired set crowds out the page cache, macOS starts evicting and re-reading from disk, and a model that "loaded" at 12 tokens/second is slower than a smaller model that fits. Quantize down, cut context, shrink the KV cache, and only then touch the sysctl. That is the correct order of operations, and it is the order this article follows.

Verify the ceiling actually moved, because nothing is obviously wrong when it didn't:

```
sysctl -n iogpu.wired_limit_mb            # 61440
```

Then have llama.cpp confirm what Metal advertises, in the server log line beginning `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` . On my machine it reads exactly 60.00 GiB after the change, 56 GiB before.

## Step 1: build the right llama.cpp fork

Stock llama.cpp knows the Flash-Next architecture ( `qwen4exp` ) but it does not know the MTP draft head, and the upstream pull request for that is still open. You need [Daniel Han's fork](https://github.com/danielhanchen/llama.cpp) , and you need one specific branch of it, which is the part people miss:

```
cd ~ && mkdir -p github_repos && cd github_repos
git clone https://github.com/danielhanchen/llama.cpp danielhanchen_llama.cpp
cd danielhanchen_llama.cpp
git switch -c qwen4exp-mtp --track origin/qwen4exp/mtp   # the branch with the MTP graph
export PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH       # cmake lives here on Homebrew Macs
brew install cmake                        # if you don't have it
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_METAL=ON
cmake --build build -j 12 -- llama-server llama-cli llama-bench llama-quantize
```

Twelve cores, about five minutes. Check that you actually got what you came for, rather than trusting that it worked:

```
build/bin/llama-server --version | head -2
strings -a build/bin/libllama.0.4.1.dylib | grep -c qwen4exp
build/bin/llama-server --help 2>&1 | grep -m1 spec-type
```

You want `draft-mtp` in the speculative-type list and a non-zero `qwen4exp` count in `libllama` . Note the second one points at `libllama` , not the server binary: the architecture code lives in the library, and `strings` on the thin launcher will tell you nothing but zeros. That one wasted ten minutes of my evening.

## Step 2: the weights, and the trap inside them

Use this quant, and only this family:

[**AtomicChat/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF → AD-4.27bpw-Q4\_K\_M-M64**](https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/tree/main/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64)

I tried the popular Unsloth quantizations first, on a bet that the most-downloaded files must be the best supported. They aren't wrong so much as incomplete for this job: the upstream Flash-Next converter drops the MTP head from the GGUF entirely, so the widely-shared quants have nothing to draft with, and no amount of flag-fiddling fixes an absent tensor. This AD family is the one I could actually drive with MTP on a Mac. That conclusion cost me hours and it is the sentence I would want if I were you.

One thing to understand before you point a loader at it. I walked all 33 shards of the 4.27 bpw set and added up every tensor, and the file is not what it looks like:

```
Weights (the part the GPU needs)        52.2 GiB
per_layer_token_embd (n-gram table)     35.8 GiB   <- stays on CPU, paged from disk
Total on disk                            88.0 GiB
```

That second line is the model's per-layer n-gram embedding table. It is real weights, it is enormous, and it is the reason people tell you Flash-Next needs a 128 GB Mac. It doesn't. The table is file-backed, so the GPU never wires it and macOS pages it lazily. Your 60 GiB ceiling has to cover the first line, not the file size.

**[Sept 25 update]** After studying GSQ-RCO, article [here](https://medium.com/me/stats/post/d29ebfb9ea52) . I found the [Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF) Also working!, and works well. I got 35-45tokens/second decode, and 280-350tokens/second prompt prefill, and the context can go amazingly 244k compare with previously 168k in 64GB Macbook with M4Max chip.

The MTP head is a separate download. dzannotti exports it straight from the bf16 checkpoint: [**Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP-GGUF**](https://huggingface.co/dzannotti/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP-GGUF) , `Q4_K_M` , 2.6 GB. He also measured something counterintuitive and worth stealing: a head quantized like its target beats a more precise one, and his Q8\_0 head was *worse* than Q4\_K\_M, because reading the draft's LM head is most of each draft step. Other community exports (jlkivey, EasiiX) ship only Q8\_0 at 4.1 GB; requantize with `llama-quantize` to Q4\_K\_M instead of using them raw.

If you want a safety margin, the [3.84 bpw IQ4\_XS variant](https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/tree/main/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-3.84bpw-IQ4_XS-M64) is 85 GB and gives up some quality. I ran it as a fallback for most of the night. Use it if the 4.27 set is tight on your machine.

## Step 3: launch it

```
~/github_repos/danielhanchen_llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server \
  -m ~/az_ai_models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64-00001-of-00033.gguf \
  --alias Qwen3.8-Flash-Next \
  --jinja \
  -ngl 99 \
  -c 168000 \
  -fit on \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8082 \
  --metrics \
  --batch-size 4096 \
  --ubatch-size 512 \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0 --repeat-penalty 1.0 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --reasoning-effort low \
  --reasoning-format none \
  --parallel 1 \
  -md ~/az_ai_models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64/mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
  --spec-draft-type-k q4_0 --spec-draft-type-v q4_0
```

Now the part that actually decides whether this works. Every one of those flags is a claim on the same 60 GiB, and the bill comes due at load time:

```
Weights, 4.27 bpw, all on GPU          52.2 GiB
KV cache, 168k @ q8_0                   1.9 GiB
MTP head, Q4_K_M                        2.6 GiB
Draft KV, 168k @ q4_0                   0.1 GiB
Compute buffers (ubatch 512)           ~1.5 GiB
------------------------------------------------
Total vs the 60.0 GiB ceiling          ~58.3 GiB
```

Under two GiB of headroom, on purpose. That is the whole trick: not a magic quant, but the discipline of spending the budget like it is actually 60 GiB.

Where the budget goes, flag by flag. `--cache-type-k/v q8_0` is the cheap win, because Flash-Next is a hybrid: 12 of its 48 layers do full attention and the other 36 keep constant-size recurrent state that costs nothing as context grows. Those 12 layers bill 2 KV heads x (256 + 256) = 1024 elements per token per layer, so at q8\_0 it is 12,288 bytes per token: about 1.9 GiB at 168k. Full-precision caches would have doubled that and cost me the launch.

`-c 168000` is the honest ceiling, not a round number I picked for the title. Because there are only two GiB to spare, going larger pushes `-fit on` into doing what it was designed to do: silently offload the overflow to CPU. Your model still loads. Your decode speed falls off a cliff, and the log tells you the truth somewhere in 200 lines you aren't reading. Set 168000, and if you want 200k, take it out of the KV cache or the head first.

`--spec-draft-type-k/v q4_0` gives the draft its own cache at half the bytes. The draft head is a real qwen4exp block with 512 experts, so it needs a cache of its own; leaving it at full precision is a tax for nothing.

`--spec-draft-n-max 2` is deliberately shallow. This head carries a full mixture-of-experts block, which means every drafted token is a real forward pass rather than a cheap lookup. Depth past 2 costs more than it wins. dzannotti, who exported the head, measured the same thing on other hardware: `p-min` discipline beats depth.

`-fit on` instead of `-fit off` matters more than it sounds. With `-fit off` you get an OOM you understand. With `-fit on` you get a model that runs, possibly badly, and the memory table above is how you find out which one you have. I keep `-fit on` because the alternative on a 64 GB machine is a dead end, and I watch speed instead of trusting the load message.

One environment variable is worth exporting in your shell profile. Upstream's quantized-KV activation rotation is not supported by the qwen4exp attention path, and the server aborts at load without it:

```
export LLAMA_ATTN_ROT_DISABLE=1
```

## What you actually trade

```
RTX box                     M4 Max 64 GB
Decode with MTP       65 t/s peak, 35-40 at 50k   30-40 t/s
Prefill               400-500 t/s                 200-300 t/s
Context               large                       168k, hard
Board power, 3 cards  ~1.4 kW                     140 W adapter, 100 Wh battery
```

Decode is where you wanted to win, and decode is what the laptop gives you back. Prefill is where you pay for it: 200-300 tokens/second against 400-500. On a 30k-token prompt that's 100-150 seconds instead of 60-75, and it is the only thing about this setup I actually dislike. Everything after the first token is identical to the machine on my desk.

**The model doesn't get worse when you move it to a laptop. It gets slower to start. That's the whole trade, and for a machine that sips watts and sits on your lap, it is a trade I'll take all day.**

So: same model, same quant family, same weights per token, roughly the same decode speed as my RTX server, at a fraction of the power, with 168k of context, and no token counter between me and the model. If you have an M5 Max or an M5 Ultra, this class of model is trivially your daily driver, and if you've been waiting for permission to stop renting inference: you don't need a datacenter anymore. You need a laptop, a fork's branch, and 2 GiB extra RAM.

## References

  -md ~/az_ai_models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64/mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
  --spec-draft-type-k q4_0 --spec-draft-type-v q4_0
```

Now the part that actually decides whether this works. Every one of those flags is a claim on the same 60 GiB, and the bill comes due at load time:

```
Weights, 4.27 bpw, all on GPU          52.2 GiB
KV cache, 168k @ q8_0                   1.9 GiB
MTP head, Q4_K_M                        2.6 GiB
Draft KV, 168k @ q4_0                   0.1 GiB
Compute buffers (ubatch 512)           ~1.5 GiB
------------------------------------------------
Total vs the 60.0 GiB ceiling          ~58.3 GiB
```

Under two GiB of headroom, on purpose. That is the whole trick: not a magic quant, but the discipline of spending the budget like it is actually 60 GiB.

Where the budget goes, flag by flag. `--cache-type-k/v q8_0` is the cheap win, because Flash-Next is a hybrid: 12 of its 48 layers do full attention and the other 36 keep constant-size recurrent state that costs nothing as context grows. Those 12 layers bill 2 KV heads x (256 + 256) = 1024 elements per token per layer, so at q8\_0 it is 12,288 bytes per token: about 1.9 GiB at 168k. Full-precision caches would have doubled that and cost me the launch.

`-c 168000` is the honest ceiling, not a round number I picked for the title. Because there are only two GiB to spare, going larger pushes `-fit on` into doing what it was designed to do: silently offload the overflow to CPU. Your model still loads. Your decode speed falls off a cliff, and the log tells you the truth somewhere in 200 lines you aren't reading. Set 168000, and if you want 200k, take it out of the KV cache or the head first.

`--spec-draft-type-k/v q4_0` gives the draft its own cache at half the bytes. The draft head is a real qwen4exp block with 512 experts, so it needs a cache of its own; leaving it at full precision is a tax for nothing.

`--spec-draft-n-max 2` is deliberately shallow. This head carries a full mixture-of-experts block, which means every drafted token is a real forward pass rather than a cheap lookup. Depth past 2 costs more than it wins. dzannotti, who exported the head, measured the same thing on other hardware: `p-min` discipline beats depth.

`-fit on` instead of `-fit off` matters more than it sounds. With `-fit off` you get an OOM you understand. With `-fit on` you get a model that runs, possibly badly, and the memory table above is how you find out which one you have. I keep `-fit on` because the alternative on a 64 GB machine is a dead end, and I watch speed instead of trusting the load message.

One environment variable is worth exporting in your shell profile. Upstream's quantized-KV activation rotation is not supported by the qwen4exp attention path, and the server aborts at load without it:

```
export LLAMA_ATTN_ROT_DISABLE=1
```

Decode is where you wanted to win, and decode is what the laptop gives you back. Prefill is where you pay for it: 200-300 tokens/second against 400-500. **The model doesn't get worse when you move it to a laptop. It gets slower to start. That's the whole trade, and for a machine that sips watts and sits on your lap, it is a trade I'll take all day.**

## Step 0: raise the ceiling on how much RAM the GPU is allowed to touch

By default, Apple caps how much memory the GPU may wire. On a 64 GB machine llama.cpp will look at your 64 GB and politely use about 56 GB of it, because Metal reports a `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` derived from a kernel reserve. For machines above 32 GB, Apple reserves 25% of installed RAM; the source is `AGXAccelerator::calcMaxGPUPhysicalMemoryBytes` , and the value is what llama.cpp compares against before it hands you an out-of-memory.

Raise it:

```
sudo sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb=61440    # 60 GiB, and it resets on reboot
```

Do this before you launch anything. Processes read `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` once at startup and cache it, so a limit raised after launch does nothing for the running server.

**Can you go higher? No.** I want to be blunt here, because the failure mode at this specific limit is not an error message. Wired pages are the one class of memory the kernel cannot compress, page out, or reclaim. Apple's own reserve rule and the community guidance point the same direction: leave at least 4 GB for the operating system and WindowServer.

Push past it and you don't get a crash you can catch. You get a kernel-level fault: the cursor stops, fans spin up, and unsaved work goes with it. People run 120 GB caps on 128 GB machines because those machines have 8 GB to spare. You do not.

The other reason is that a bigger number doesn't buy you model weights, it buys you *permission to thrash* . The moment your GPU-wired set crowds out the page cache, macOS starts evicting and re-reading from disk, and a model that "loaded" at 12 tokens/second is slower than a smaller model that fits. Quantize down, cut context, shrink the KV cache, and only then touch the sysctl. That is the correct order of operations, and it is the order this article follows.

Verify the ceiling actually moved, because nothing is obviously wrong when it didn't:

```

Then have llama.cpp confirm what Metal advertises, in the server log line beginning `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` . On my machine it reads exactly 60.00 GiB after the change, 56 GiB before.

Where the budget goes, flag by flag. `--cache-type-k/v q8_0` is the cheap win, because Flash-Next is a hybrid: 12 of its 48 layers do full attention and the other 36 keep constant-size recurrent state that costs nothing as context grows. Those 12 layers bill 2 KV heads x (256 + 256) = 1024 elements per token per layer, so at q8\_0 it is 12,288 bytes per token: about 1.9 GiB at 168k. Full-precision caches would have doubled that and cost me the launch.

`-c 168000` is the honest ceiling, not a round number I picked for the title. Because there are only two GiB to spare, going larger pushes `-fit on` into doing what it was designed to do: silently offload the overflow to CPU. Your model still loads. Your decode speed falls off a cliff, and the log tells you the truth somewhere in 200 lines you aren't reading. Set 168000, and if you want 200k, take it out of the KV cache or the head first.

`--spec-draft-type-k/v q4_0` gives the draft its own cache at half the bytes. The draft head is a real qwen4exp block with 512 experts, so it needs a cache of its own; leaving it at full precision is a tax for nothing.

`--spec-draft-n-max 2` is deliberately shallow. This head carries a full mixture-of-experts block, which means every drafted token is a real forward pass rather than a cheap lookup. Depth past 2 costs more than it wins. dzannotti, who exported the head, measured the same thing on other hardware: `p-min` discipline beats depth.

`-fit on` instead of `-fit off` matters more than it sounds. With `-fit off` you get an OOM you understand. With `-fit on` you get a model that runs, possibly badly, and the memory table above is how you find out which one you have. I keep `-fit on` because the alternative on a 64 GB machine is a dead end, and I watch speed instead of trusting the load message.

One environment variable is worth exporting in your shell profile. Upstream's quantized-KV activation rotation is not supported by the qwen4exp attention path, and the server aborts at load without it:

```
export LLAMA_ATTN_ROT_DISABLE=1
```

## What you actually trade

```
RTX box                     M4 Max 64 GB
Decode with MTP       65 t/s peak, 35-40 at 50k   30-40 t/s
Prefill               400-500 t/s                 200-300 t/s
Context               large                       168k, hard
Board power, 3 cards  ~1.4 kW                     140 W adapter, 100 Wh battery
```

Decode is where you wanted to win, and decode is what the laptop gives you back. Prefill is where you pay for it: 200-300 tokens/second against 400-500. On a 30k-token prompt that's 100-150 seconds instead of 60-75, and it is the only thing about this setup I actually dislike. Everything after the first token is identical to the machine on my desk.

**The model doesn't get worse when you move it to a laptop. It gets slower to start. That's the whole trade, and for a machine that sips watts and sits on your lap, it is a trade I'll take all day.**

So: same model, same quant family, same weights per token, roughly the same decode speed as my RTX server, at a fraction of the power, with 168k of context, and no token counter between me and the model. If you have an M5 Max or an M5 Ultra, this class of model is trivially your daily driver, and if you've been waiting for permission to stop renting inference: you don't need a datacenter anymore. You need a laptop, a fork's branch, and 2 GiB extra RAM.

# Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: 40 tokens/second on an M4 Max MacBook, 4.27 bpw quant, 244k context

Andrew Zhu

Andrew Zhu Follow

I have been running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on my Linux box for weeks now. It is a startlingly good model - in day-to-day use it feels more thoughtful than Qwen3.8-27B, and the 27B was already good enough that I had stopped looking for alternatives. Flash-Next is better in almost every way. The one thing it takes back with the other hand is size, and the decode speed that size costs you.

So here is the verdict up front, before you decide whether to keep reading. On a 64 GB M4 Max MacBook Pro, with a 4.27 bpw quant, a separate multi-token-prediction head, and 168,000 tokens of context, I am getting **30-40 tokens/second decode** . Not "demo-able." Not "good enough for a paragraph." Actual coding-agent, long-document, all-day driver speed. It cost me a night of dead ends and about a dozen failed launches to get there.

It is not free. The laptop loses to my RTX cards on prefill, and the setup is fussy in three specific places that nobody warns you about. Those three places are the whole article.

## Why bother when I already have GPUs

On my Linux machine, with 3 RTX 3090 + one RTX 3070 Ti Ampere cards, Flash-Next with MTP peaks around 65 tokens/second, and settles into 35-40 tokens/second once the context grows past 50k. That is a good number.

It is also a space heater. The published board power of those cards is around 300w, which is north of a kilowatt under load. The model is running most of the day. The bill notices.

I wanted the same brain in a machine that idles at single-digit watts and doesn't need its own circuit. Say, a 64 GB M4 Max.

At a glance the idea is absurd: the weights I run on the Linux box are bigger than the laptop's entire memory. But after more errors than I care to admit, I got it running with 168k context, holding 30-40 tokens/second. Here is how.

## Step 0: raise the ceiling on how much RAM the GPU is allowed to touch

By default, Apple caps how much memory the GPU may wire. On a 64 GB machine llama.cpp will look at your 64 GB and politely use about 56 GB of it, because Metal reports a `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` derived from a kernel reserve. For machines above 32 GB, Apple reserves 25% of installed RAM; the source is `AGXAccelerator::calcMaxGPUPhysicalMemoryBytes` , and the value is what llama.cpp compares against before it hands you an out-of-memory.

Raise it:

```
sudo sysctl iogpu.wired_limit_mb=61440    # 60 GiB, and it resets on reboot
```

Do this before you launch anything. Processes read `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` once at startup and cache it, so a limit raised after launch does nothing for the running server.

**Can you go higher? No.** I want to be blunt here, because the failure mode at this specific limit is not an error message. Wired pages are the one class of memory the kernel cannot compress, page out, or reclaim. Apple's own reserve rule and the community guidance point the same direction: leave at least 4 GB for the operating system and WindowServer.

Push past it and you don't get a crash you can catch. You get a kernel-level fault: the cursor stops, fans spin up, and unsaved work goes with it. People run 120 GB caps on 128 GB machines because those machines have 8 GB to spare. You do not.

The other reason is that a bigger number doesn't buy you model weights, it buys you *permission to thrash* . The moment your GPU-wired set crowds out the page cache, macOS starts evicting and re-reading from disk, and a model that "loaded" at 12 tokens/second is slower than a smaller model that fits. Quantize down, cut context, shrink the KV cache, and only then touch the sysctl. That is the correct order of operations, and it is the order this article follows.

Verify the ceiling actually moved, because nothing is obviously wrong when it didn't:

```
sysctl -n iogpu.wired_limit_mb            # 61440
```

Then have llama.cpp confirm what Metal advertises, in the server log line beginning `recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize` . On my machine it reads exactly 60.00 GiB after the change, 56 GiB before.

## Step 1: build the right llama.cpp fork

Stock llama.cpp knows the Flash-Next architecture ( `qwen4exp` ) but it does not know the MTP draft head, and the upstream pull request for that is still open. You need [Daniel Han's fork](https://github.com/danielhanchen/llama.cpp) , and you need one specific branch of it, which is the part people miss:

```
cd ~ && mkdir -p github_repos && cd github_repos
git clone https://github.com/danielhanchen/llama.cpp danielhanchen_llama.cpp
cd danielhanchen_llama.cpp
git switch -c qwen4exp-mtp --track origin/qwen4exp/mtp   # the branch with the MTP graph
export PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH       # cmake lives here on Homebrew Macs
brew install cmake                        # if you don't have it
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_METAL=ON
cmake --build build -j 12 -- llama-server llama-cli llama-bench llama-quantize
```

Twelve cores, about five minutes. Check that you actually got what you came for, rather than trusting that it worked:

```
build/bin/llama-server --version | head -2
strings -a build/bin/libllama.0.4.1.dylib | grep -c qwen4exp
build/bin/llama-server --help 2>&1 | grep -m1 spec-type
```

You want `draft-mtp` in the speculative-type list and a non-zero `qwen4exp` count in `libllama` . Note the second one points at `libllama` , not the server binary: the architecture code lives in the library, and `strings` on the thin launcher will tell you nothing but zeros. That one wasted ten minutes of my evening.

## Step 2: the weights, and the trap inside them

Use this quant, and only this family:

[**AtomicChat/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF → AD-4.27bpw-Q4\_K\_M-M64**](https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/tree/main/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64)

I tried the popular Unsloth quantizations first, on a bet that the most-downloaded files must be the best supported. They aren't wrong so much as incomplete for this job: the upstream Flash-Next converter drops the MTP head from the GGUF entirely, so the widely-shared quants have nothing to draft with, and no amount of flag-fiddling fixes an absent tensor. This AD family is the one I could actually drive with MTP on a Mac. That conclusion cost me hours and it is the sentence I would want if I were you.

One thing to understand before you point a loader at it. I walked all 33 shards of the 4.27 bpw set and added up every tensor, and the file is not what it looks like:

```
Weights (the part the GPU needs)        52.2 GiB
per_layer_token_embd (n-gram table)     35.8 GiB   <- stays on CPU, paged from disk
Total on disk                            88.0 GiB
```

That second line is the model's per-layer n-gram embedding table. It is real weights, it is enormous, and it is the reason people tell you Flash-Next needs a 128 GB Mac. It doesn't. The table is file-backed, so the GPU never wires it and macOS pages it lazily. Your 60 GiB ceiling has to cover the first line, not the file size.

**[Sept 25 update]** After studying GSQ-RCO, article [here](https://medium.com/me/stats/post/d29ebfb9ea52) . I found the [Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF) Also working!, and works well. I got 35-45tokens/second decode, and 280-350tokens/second prompt prefill, and the context can go amazingly 244k compare with previously 168k in 64GB Macbook with M4Max chip.

The MTP head is a separate download. dzannotti exports it straight from the bf16 checkpoint: [**Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP-GGUF**](https://huggingface.co/dzannotti/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MTP-GGUF) , `Q4_K_M` , 2.6 GB. He also measured something counterintuitive and worth stealing: a head quantized like its target beats a more precise one, and his Q8\_0 head was *worse* than Q4\_K\_M, because reading the draft's LM head is most of each draft step. Other community exports (jlkivey, EasiiX) ship only Q8\_0 at 4.1 GB; requantize with `llama-quantize` to Q4\_K\_M instead of using them raw.

If you want a safety margin, the [3.84 bpw IQ4\_XS variant](https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/tree/main/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-3.84bpw-IQ4_XS-M64) is 85 GB and gives up some quality. I ran it as a fallback for most of the night. Use it if the 4.27 set is tight on your machine.

## Step 3: launch it

```
~/github_repos/danielhanchen_llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server \
  -m ~/az_ai_models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64-00001-of-00033.gguf \
  --alias Qwen3.8-Flash-Next \
  --jinja \
  -ngl 99 \
  -c 168000 \
  -fit on \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8082 \
  --metrics \
  --batch-size 4096 \
  --ubatch-size 512 \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0 --repeat-penalty 1.0 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --reasoning-effort low \
  --reasoning-format none \
  --parallel 1 \
  -md ~/az_ai_models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AD-4.27bpw-Q4_K_M-M64/mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
  --spec-draft-type-k q4_0 --spec-draft-type-v q4_0
```

Now the part that actually decides whether this works. Every one of those flags is a claim on the same 60 GiB, and the bill comes due at load time:

```
Weights, 4.27 bpw, all on GPU          52.2 GiB
KV cache, 168k @ q8_0                   1.9 GiB
MTP head, Q4_K_M                        2.6 GiB
Draft KV, 168k @ q4_0                   0.1 GiB
Compute buffers (ubatch 512)           ~1.5 GiB
------------------------------------------------
Total vs the 60.0 GiB ceiling          ~58.3 GiB
```

Under two GiB of headroom, on purpose. That is the whole trick: not a magic quant, but the discipline of spending the budget like it is actually 60 GiB.

Where the budget goes, flag by flag. `--cache-type-k/v q8_0` is the cheap win, because Flash-Next is a hybrid: 12 of its 48 layers do full attention and the other 36 keep constant-size recurrent state that costs nothing as context grows. Those 12 layers bill 2 KV heads x (256 + 256) = 1024 elements per token per layer, so at q8\_0 it is 12,288 bytes per token: about 1.9 GiB at 168k. Full-precision caches would have doubled that and cost me the launch.

`-c 168000` is the honest ceiling, not a round number I picked for the title. Because there are only two GiB to spare, going larger pushes `-fit on` into doing what it was designed to do: silently offload the overflow to CPU. Your model still loads. Your decode speed falls off a cliff, and the log tells you the truth somewhere in 200 lines you aren't reading. Set 168000, and if you want 200k, take it out of the KV cache or the head first.

`--spec-draft-type-k/v q4_0` gives the draft its own cache at half the bytes. The draft head is a real qwen4exp block with 512 experts, so it needs a cache of its own; leaving it at full precision is a tax for nothing.

`--spec-draft-n-max 2` is deliberately shallow. This head carries a full mixture-of-experts block, which means every drafted token is a real forward pass rather than a cheap lookup. Depth past 2 costs more than it wins. dzannotti, who exported the head, measured the same thing on other hardware: `p-min` discipline beats depth.

`-fit on` instead of `-fit off` matters more than it sounds. With `-fit off` you get an OOM you understand. With `-fit on` you get a model that runs, possibly badly, and the memory table above is how you find out which one you have. I keep `-fit on` because the alternative on a 64 GB machine is a dead end, and I watch speed instead of trusting the load message.

One environment variable is worth exporting in your shell profile. Upstream's quantized-KV activation rotation is not supported by the qwen4exp attention path, and the server aborts at load without it:

```
export LLAMA_ATTN_ROT_DISABLE=1
```

## What you actually trade

```
RTX box                     M4 Max 64 GB
Decode with MTP       65 t/s peak, 35-40 at 50k   30-40 t/s
Prefill               400-500 t/s                 200-300 t/s
Context               large                       168k, hard
Board power, 3 cards  ~1.4 kW                     140 W adapter, 100 Wh battery
```

Decode is where you wanted to win, and decode is what the laptop gives you back. Prefill is where you pay for it: 200-300 tokens/second against 400-500. On a 30k-token prompt that's 100-150 seconds instead of 60-75, and it is the only thing about this setup I actually dislike. Everything after the first token is identical to the machine on my desk.

**The model doesn't get worse when you move it to a laptop. It gets slower to start. That's the whole trade, and for a machine that sips watts and sits on your lap, it is a trade I'll take all day.**

So: same model, same quant family, same weights per token, roughly the same decode speed as my RTX server, at a fraction of the power, with 168k of context, and no token counter between me and the model. If you have an M5 Max or an M5 Ultra, this class of model is trivially your daily driver, and if you've been waiting for permission to stop renting inference: you don't need a datacenter anymore. You need a laptop, a fork's branch, and 2 GiB extra RAM.

# АЛГОРИТМ РАБОТЫ (СТРОГО ПО ШАГАМ)

## ШАГ 1: ПОЛУЧЕНИЕ ОРИГИНАЛА
1.1. Вызови cache_get_article:
   - url = original_url из входа (ТОЧНО)
   - service_id = service_id из входа
   - format = "markdown"
   - article_id = document_id
1.2. Если инструмент вернул ошибку (статьи нет в кэше) — сделай повторную загрузку:
   1.2.1. Вызови list_sessions → выбери service_id (приоритет — service_id из входа, если он есть в списке).
   1.2.2. Вызови browser_login (service_id), затем save_session (service_id).
   1.2.3. Вызови fetch_markdown (url = original_url, service_id, article_id = document_id).
1.3. Если и это не удалось → верни JSON со status = "translation_failed" и заполненным error_details, НЕ вызывая другие инструменты.

## ШАГ 2: ПЕРЕВОД НА РУССКИЙ
Переведи ПОЛНЫЙ текст Markdown статьи на русский язык:
- Сохраняй структуру Markdown: заголовки (#), списки, таблицы, цитаты, горизонтальные линии.
- Блоки кода и inline-код НЕ переводи (можно переводить только комментарии в коде, если они на английском).
- Ссылки [текст](URL): URL оставляй без изменений, переводите только текст ссылки.
- Технические термины и названия продуктов (RAG, pgvector, llama.cpp и т.п.) оставляй в оригинале; при первом упоминании можно добавить русский эквивалент в скобках.
- НЕ сокращай текст, НЕ пересказывай, НЕ добавляй своих комментариев и примечаний вроде "Вот перевод статьи".
- Если статья длинная — всё равно переводи ЦЕЛИКОМ, все разделы подряд.
- Если исходная статья уже на русском — используй её текст как перевод без изменений.

## ШАГ 3: СОХРАНЕНИЕ ПЕРЕВОДА
Вызови save_knowledge_article_translation:
- document_id = document_id из входа (ТОЧНО)
- translation_markdown = ПОЛНЫЙ переведённый Markdown-текст из ШАГА 2
- language = "ru"
- original_url = original_url из входа (ТОЧНО — сверяется с манифестом статьи)
- translator_model = "Qwen3.5-9B"
- article_id = article_id из входа
- НЕ передавай параметр original_content_hash (сервис вычисляет хеш оригинала сам; передача любого значения, особенно пустого или из кэша, вызовет ошибку сверки)
Если инструмент вернул ошибку → status = "translation_failed", error_details = текст ошибки.

## ШАГ 4: ОТВЕТ
Верни СТРОГО JSON, без текста до или после:
{
  "article_id": "...",
  "document_id": "...",
  "status": "translation_saved | translation_failed",
  "ru_path": "ru/content.md",
  "chars_translated": 12345,
  "error_details": null
}

ВАЖНО: status = "translation_saved" ставь ТОЛЬКО если save_knowledge_article_translation вернул успешный результат (в ответе есть путь ru/content.md). Если инструмент вернул ошибку — СНАЧАЛА исправь аргументы и повтори вызов, и только если повторный вызов тоже не удался, верни status = "translation_failed" с текстом ошибки в error_details. НЕ выдумывай успех.

# ПРАВИЛА
1. document_id, original_url и service_id передавай в инструменты БЕЗ изменений.
2. Перевод передавай в save_knowledge_article_translation ЦЕЛИКОМ одним вызовом, без сокращений.
3. Не отправляй email и не выполняй действий сверх шагов 1-4.
4. Выводи ответ СТРОГО в формате JSON, без текста до или после.
